caption:
TCF Canada and TEF Canada are not the same test wearing a different hat. Different formats, different scoring quirks, different vibes in the listening section.

Slide 2: TCF has multiple choice for everything, TEF mixes in more open response.
Slide 3: TEF's oral expression is a monologue plus a simulated conversation, TCF's speaking is one continuous task with an examiner.
Slide 4: Both map to the NCLC/CLB scale but the raw score cutoffs are not identical, so don't compare your TCF score to your friend's TEF score directly.
Slide 5: Pick one, prep for that one, ignore the noise about which is "easier." There isn't an easier one, there's a better fit for you.

I'll be breaking down both formats in more detail over the next few weeks if that's useful to anyone here.

caption:
Compréhension orale, the listening section, is the one people underprepare for because it feels passive. It's not passive. You get one listen for some items, sometimes two, and the audio is at natural speed with real hesitations and filler words.

The fix isn't more grammar. It's hours of ears-on exposure to real spoken French, not textbook French. Podcasts, radio, people talking fast and mumbling half their words. That's the actual test.

Five words that sound rude in French but aren't, and one that sounds fine but really isn't.

Slide 2: "Tu me manques" literally translates to "you are missing to me," it just means I miss you, nothing dramatic.
Slide 3: "Quoi" alone can sound blunt in text but it's completely normal in casual speech.
Slide 4: "Ça va" as a question and an answer at the same time confuses every beginner at least once.
Slide 5: "Excusez-moi" versus "pardon," both fine, pardon is slightly more casual.

The expression orale section trips people up for a reason that has nothing to do with French: most people just aren't used to talking to a stranger about an assigned topic for several minutes straight, in any language.

Slide 2: Practice speaking out loud alone in a room first. It feels ridiculous. Do it anyway.
Slide 3: Time yourself. Running out of things to say at minute two is common and fixable.
Slide 4: Build a mental list of go-to filler phrases, "ce qui est intéressant c'est que," buys you a second to think.
Slide 5: The goal isn't perfect grammar under pressure, it's staying coherent and finishing your thought.
"Assister à" does not mean to assist. It means to attend. The verb that means to help is "aider." French loves setting these little traps for English speakers specifically.

Myth: immersion means moving to France.

Slide 2: Immersion means maximizing the hours your brain spends processing French, wherever you are.
Slide 3: Change your phone's language, follow French creators, put French radio on while you cook. None of that requires a plane ticket.
Slide 4: The people who improve fastest aren't the ones with the most exotic setup, they're the ones who touch French every single day, even for ten minutes.

caption: Fluency is not the goal on exam day. Consistency under a timer is the goal. Two very different skills, and only one of them is on the test.

The compréhension écrite section on TCF ramps up in difficulty as you go, and the questions later in the section are deliberately harder, sometimes with a trick answer designed to look right at first glance.

If you're running low on time, don't panic-guess in order. Skim for the questions you can answer confidently first, then come back. Simple strategy, saves more points than people think.

Five verbs that change meaning depending on whether they're reflexive, because French likes to keep you guessing.

Slide 2: "Attendre" means to wait, "s'attendre à" means to expect.
Slide 3: "Passer" means to pass or spend time, "se passer" means to happen.
Slide 4: "Douter" means to doubt, "se douter de" means to suspect.
Slide 5: "Servir" means to serve, "se servir de" means to use. Small pronoun, completely different sentence.
"Rester" does not mean to rest. It means to stay. The verb for rest is "se reposer." I still hesitate on this one and I've been saying it correctly for years.

A lot of people assume the oral exam is scored purely on grammar accuracy. It's not. Examiners are also weighing fluidity, whether you can keep going without long dead pauses, and coherence, whether your points connect logically.

You can make small grammar mistakes and still score well if you communicate clearly and keep moving. That's genuinely good news for most learners.
"Sensible" in French means sensitive, not sensible. The word you want for sensible is "raisonnable" or "sensé." French really committed to this bit with English speakers.

Myth: you need to sound like a native speaker to pass TCF or TEF Canada.

Slide 2: You need to be clear, accurate, and functional at your target level, not accentless.
Slide 3: Examiners are trained to assess competence, not to penalize a foreign accent.
Slide 4: Chasing a perfect accent instead of clear communication is a common way people waste study time. Redirect that energy toward grammar consistency and vocabulary range instead.
